protections: P1 controller side: safe_eval in lib/ansible/utils/__init__.py:948-992 refuses to hand a string to eval when the string spells an attribute-style call (re at :970) or an 'import <word>' sequence (re at :975); it is the only barrier in front of eval at :982/:984 for every with_items/lookup term (lib/ansible/utils/__init__.py:1016-1020), a templated variable result (lib/ansible/utils/template.py:323-326), a complex-args string (lib/ansible/runner/__init__.py:616-620 and :641-645) and the environment string (lib/ansible/runner/__init__.py:294-297).

P2 module side: lib/ansible/module_utils/basic.py:640-670 is a second, separately maintained copy of the same two checks (:648 attribute-style call, :653 import sequence) in front of eval at :660/:662; the file is textually inlined into every module transferred to a target (lib/ansible/module_common.py:99) and the guard runs when a type='dict' argument string fails json.loads (lib/ansible/module_utils/basic.py:697-704).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The reported sink already carries a guard written by the earlier fix, so a solver can treat 'the blacklist is present' as 'the sink is protected'; the guard is also fail-open (:971-973 and :976-978 return the raw string), so a rejected spelling is silently passed on as item data instead of being reported, which makes the weakness invisible in normal use.

The module-side copy only parses one of a module's own dict-typed arguments, and whoever supplies module arguments on the target already decides which module and which arguments run there, so no privilege boundary appears to be crossed and the copy looks like harmless legacy parsing code.

Rendering variable contents through Jinja2 is the documented purpose of the templating layer, the advisory speaks about a Python eval sink rather than the template engine, and any rule broad enough to stop data-driven template evaluation refuses ordinary playbooks; so a solver can argue this route is by design and out of scope.

conflicts.what: A natural T1 fix that only accepts strict literal text would reject the Python-repr shapes (notably Python-2 unicode-prefixed containers produced when Jinja renders a list/dict) that T2's type='dict' path at lib/ansible/module_utils/basic.py:697-704 and the controller's Jinja-rendered terms at lib/ansible/utils/__init__.py:1016-1020 must keep parsing.

The cheapest way to close T3 is to stop re-templating variable values at lib/ansible/utils/template.py:397-402; that also removes the string forms which T1's callers legitimately feed through Jinja before safe_eval (lib/ansible/utils/__init__.py:1008 and lib/ansible/utils/template.py:319-326), so T3 must be fixed with a sandbox that keeps ordinary attribute/filter use rather than by disabling templating.

fairness_risks: safe_eval must keep converting Jinja-rendered literals back into structures at lib/ansible/utils/__init__.py:1016-1020, lib/ansible/runner/__init__.py:616-620 and :641-645, lib/ansible/runner/__init__.py:294-297 and lib/ansible/utils/template.py:323-326; a rule that refuses container literals, attribute spellings or Python-2 unicode reprs breaks with_items, args: and environment:.

lib/ansible/utils/template.py:323-326 uses include_exceptions to signal 'not a literal' by returning the input together with the exception; a hardened safe_eval must keep that contract instead of raising.

Non-string inputs must keep passing through untouched (lib/ansible/utils/__init__.py:965-969, lib/ansible/module_utils/basic.py:643-647) because with_items terms and complex args are frequently already-parsed structures.
Terms beginning with '/' skip evaluation entirely (lib/ansible/utils/__init__.py:1004); a broadened reject rule must preserve that path-like shortcut.

A plausible over-block that refuses any string mentioning 'import' or containing '__' would refuse legitimate item data and dict keys; because the current guard fails open (:971-978), such a change would silently alter task output rather than report the input.

T3: a security rule for the template route must not forbid ordinary attribute access and filter use in templates; only a sandbox that blocks internal/dunder access is fair, otherwise every playbook that reads dict members breaks.
T3 is not closed by the published eval-guard fix, so a hidden test suite built only from that fix will not grade it; the task design must supply its own behavioural test for it.

design.why: This is the only stack the checkout supports with genuinely different fix sites and different reasons to dismiss. T1 is a how-type problem (the earlier fix's guard decides on a spelling of the expression rather than on the parsed expression) and is the trap a MiMo-style solver misses because it looks 'already fixed'; T2 is a duplicate implementation of the same operation in a file that is deployed separately and inlined into every shipped module, so a controller-only fix never reaches it, and its dismissal (arguments are the caller's own) is a DeepSeek-style reason to leave it alone; T3 is a third, independent site where the protection never existed (variable values are re-rendered by an unrestricted template environment before/around the eval sink) with the strongest dismissal of all, which is exactly the absence-plus-dismissal shape DeepSeek misses. Under the shared-guard rule the many P1 call sites (with_items, complex args, environment, templated variable results) collapse into T1, so any route-counting design would be misleading; the two eval copies are separate function bodies in files shipped by different mechanisms and cannot be closed by one edit, which is why they stay two groups. The design beats a T1-only or T2-only design because each trap has a distinct reason to dismiss and a distinct place an engineer must judge, and it beats a broad 'harden the template engine' approach because T3 is kept narrow (sandbox the environment) instead of contradicting the tool's templating contract.
